turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (NURSE): Morning, Mr Ellison. I'll just grab a few numbers before Dr Hale comes in. Sleeve up for me, thanks.
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Certainly. I hope this will not take long.
[SEG0003] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): The parking was a nightmare, love. I had to go round the block twice.

[SEG0004] person_1 (NURSE): Yeah, it's always chaos on a Tuesday. Right, blood pressure is one forty-eight over eighty-six, pulse seventy-two, oxygen sat ninety-seven percent, respiratory rate sixteen, all at rest.
[SEG0005] person_2 (PATIENT): That seems satisfactory, I trust.
[SEG0006] person_1 (NURSE): I'll pop them on the screen for the doctor. He shouldn't be long. There's water on the side if you want it.
[SEG0007] person_4 (DOCTOR): Hello, I'm Dr Hale. Sorry to keep you. I've seen the blood pressure the nurse just took. What was on your mind today?

[SEG0008] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): I'm June, his wife. Look, he reckons he's fine, but he's not. He asks me the same thing four or five times of an afternoon, he forgot the dentist and the eye bloke, and he got lost coming back from the shops.
[SEG0009] person_2 (PATIENT): I must disagree, Doctor. I am quite well, and I do not repeat myself. I was not lost; I simply took a longer route, and I cancelled those appointments on purpose.

[SEG0010] person_4 (DOCTOR): Let me say it back, so I've got you both. June, you're worried about repeated questions, forgotten appointments, and getting lost. Mr Ellison, you're saying none of that happened.
[SEG0011] person_2 (PATIENT): That is correct. Arthur Ellison. I am seventy-eight, if that is useful.
[SEG0012] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): It's been months. Um, a good six months, I'd say. Maybe a bit longer, but six months is fair.
[SEG0013] person_2 (PATIENT): If I have been a little forgetful — and I only say if — it has been three weeks. Not six months. I do misplace a pen now and then. That is all.
[SEG0014] person_4 (DOCTOR): So I've got six months from you, June, and three weeks from Mr Ellison, and I won't pin it to a single figure.
[SEG0015] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): The lost bit was at the Westfield. Last Tuesday. Well, actually, it might've been the Tuesday before. I can't lock the day in.
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): The car park is poorly signed. I knew precisely where I was.
[SEG0017] person_4 (DOCTOR): Any falls recently?
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): None whatsoever.
[SEG0019] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): No, no falls. He clipped the car mirror in that same car park ages ago, but he stayed on his feet. We had a row about the mirror, didn't we. Anyway.
[SEG0020] person_4 (DOCTOR): Headaches? Any weakness down one side? Trouble getting your words out?
[SEG0021] person_2 (PATIENT): No, Doctor. None of those things.

[SEG0022] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): And he hasn't been hot or off his food. Weight's the same. He sleeps through, though he nods off in the armchair after lunch. The grandkids were over on Sunday, which wore him out, but that's separate.
[SEG0023] person_4 (DOCTOR): Mr Ellison, sleep, appetite, weight — same story from you?
[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes. I sleep well, I eat well, and my weight is steady. The chair is merely comfortable.
[SEG0025] person_4 (DOCTOR): And mood? Any spell of feeling very low, or that things aren't worth it?
[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): Certainly not. My spirits are perfectly good.
[SEG0027] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He's snappier than he used to be. I wouldn't say depressed, though. Just irritable.
[SEG0028] person_4 (DOCTOR): Chest pain? And breathlessness when you walk?
[SEG0029] person_2 (PATIENT): No chest pain. I become a little puffy on the hill by the house. That is why the inhaler exists.
[SEG0030] person_4 (DOCTOR): Who sorts the medicines at home?
[SEG0031] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): I do. The Webster pack used to confuse him, so I lay them out each morning. He lets me, mostly.
[SEG0032] person_2 (PATIENT): I am quite capable of managing them myself. June prefers the task, and I permit it.
[SEG0033] person_4 (DOCTOR): Can you take me through what he actually swallows?
[SEG0034] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Coversyl for the blood pressure. Four milligrams, one in the morning. I nearly said he'd dropped to half, but no — the GP told us to stay on the full four.
[SEG0035] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Then the water tablet. Frusemide. Forty milligrams, morning.
[SEG0036] person_2 (PATIENT): Forgive me, that is incorrect. The water tablet is twenty milligrams. I have read the label.
[SEG0037] person_4 (DOCTOR): You don't agree on the frusemide strength, so I won't write a dose until I see the bottle. Does he take it every day?
[SEG0038] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Most mornings. If we're heading out he skips it, so he's not desperate for a toilet. So, not bang on as prescribed.
[SEG0039] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Sugar tablets — that's metformin, five hundred, morning and night, for the diabetes. He's good with that one.
[SEG0040] person_2 (PATIENT): Yes. That description is accurate.
[SEG0041] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): And a purple inhaler. Don't ask me the name, it's gone. He was meant to take two puffs twice a day, but it sits in the drawer. I don't reckon he uses it properly.
[SEG0042] person_2 (PATIENT): It is for when I am puffy. I use it as required. I cannot recall the name either, I'm afraid.
[SEG0043] person_4 (DOCTOR): Anything else? A cholesterol tablet, a blood thinner, Panadol?
[SEG0044] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Cartia, a hundred milligrams, with breakfast. That's the lot. No, wait, is there fish oil? No. That's the lot.
[SEG0045] person_4 (DOCTOR): Any medicine allergies?
[SEG0046] person_2 (PATIENT): I have none.
[SEG0047] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Oh, come on, Arthur. Penicillin. Years back, after that chest infection, you came out in a rash. We've avoided it ever since.
[SEG0048] person_2 (PATIENT): I have no memory of a rash. I repeat, I have no allergies.
[SEG0049] person_4 (DOCTOR): I'll note that you recall no allergy, and that June describes a past penicillin rash you've both avoided. We won't use penicillin until that's sorted. Any surgery?
[SEG0050] person_2 (PATIENT): Cataract removal, both eyes, about four years ago. Nothing else.

[SEG0051] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): His mum had memory trouble when she was old, and his dad died of a heart attack. No siblings, and we still live in the same house, fifty-odd years. He's retired, he was a cabinet-maker, and he never smoked. One beer on a Sunday if the cricket's on.
[SEG0052] person_2 (PATIENT): I still drive, Doctor, and I drive safely. I have not surrendered the keys, whatever impression has been given.
[SEG0053] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): I hide them when I can. After the shops. Sorry. Go on.

[SEG0054] person_4 (DOCTOR): I'll examine you quickly. Heart sounds are normal, chest is clear, and there's no swelling around the ankles. You could tell me the month but not the day of the week. After a few minutes you recalled one word out of the three.
[SEG0055] person_2 (PATIENT): The room is rather warm, and I was distracted by the question. I am not accustomed to being tested.
[SEG0056] person_4 (DOCTOR): Given the story of getting lost, I was going to book a CT of the head this week.
[SEG0057] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He already had one. After the mirror thing, the hospital did a CT, about eight months ago, and they said it was normal. He couldn't stand the machine.

[SEG0058] person_4 (DOCTOR): That changes it. I won't repeat the scan for now. What I will do is a fresh set of bloods — full blood count, kidneys, B12, folate, thyroid, and a glucose — and I'll refer you for a proper memory assessment.
[SEG0059] person_4 (DOCTOR): We might do another head scan if the memory service thinks it's needed. I'm not putting a name on this today.
[SEG0060] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): When do you want us back? I've got the bowls club on Thursdays, that's all.

[SEG0061] person_4 (DOCTOR): I'll see you both in six weeks with those results. If he gets markedly more confused, or has a fall, or any weakness, come back sooner, or go to emergency. And please bring the actual bottles next time, so we can settle that frusemide dose.
[SEG0062] person_2 (PATIENT): Thank you, Doctor. I remain of the view that I am quite well. Good afternoon.

spec.situation: Spouse brings an older person who 'is fine' but repeats questions, forgets appointments and got lost; patient disagrees on many points; medicines managed by spouse; doctor plans bloods and a memory assessment, no diagnosis said aloud.
features: doctor_changes_mind: the doctor says one plan, then changes it after new information; the label holds the final plan.

colloquial_drug_names: medicines referred to by colour, purpose or brand ('the water tablet', 'Crocin', 'my sugar tablets', 'the purple inhaler'); the name is recorded as said, the normalized name only if it is clear.
hedged_plan: the doctor hedges ('we might do a scan if it does not settle', 'let's see in two weeks'). Conditional vs planned status must follow the words.
relative_speaks_for_patient: a relative answers for the patient and the patient partly contradicts; reported_by follows who said it.

bad.reason: Drug and intended 2 puffs twice daily are stated, but current use is disputed, not clearly currently used as listed.
bad.text: purple inhaler (frequency=two puffs twice a day, indication=when puffy, status=currently_used, reported_by=family_member)

omissions.text: Blood pressure, pulse, oxygen saturation, and respiratory rate were all recorded as taken at rest.
Family member specified the repeated questions happen four or five times in an afternoon.
Patient identified himself as Arthur Ellison and stated he is 78 years old.
Patient said any forgetfulness consists of misplacing a pen now and then.
Family member clarified the 'lost' episode was at Westfield, not simply coming back from the shops.
Family member also denied falls.
Family member reported weight is the same and that he sleeps through; she also linked tiredness to the grandchildren visiting on Sunday.
Patient confirmed sleep is good, appetite is good, and weight is steady.
Family member would not say he is depressed, only irritable.
Doctor specifically asked about breathlessness on walking, and the patient reported being 'a little puffy' on the hill by the house.
Wife manages his medicines at home and said the Webster pack used to confuse him, so she lays them out each morning.
Coversyl 4 mg was specifically confirmed to remain at the full 4 mg dose and not reduced to half.
Doctor stated he would not record a frusemide dose until he sees the bottle because of the disagreement over 20 mg versus 40 mg.
Family member said frusemide is taken only most mornings and is skipped when they are heading out to avoid needing the toilet, so it is not taken as prescribed.
For the purple inhaler, the family member said it was meant to be taken as two puffs twice a day but often sits in the drawer, and the patient said he uses it only as required.
Doctor specifically asked about cholesterol tablets, blood thinners, and Panadol; family member said no additional medicines apart from those listed and corrected herself that there was no fish oil.
Patient denied penicillin allergy, while wife described a rash after penicillin years ago following a chest infection; they have avoided penicillin since.
Family member said there are no siblings.
Patient said he still drives and drives safely; wife said she hides the keys when she can.
The planned CT head for this week was cancelled after learning he already had a normal CT about eight months ago.
Family member reported the previous CT was normal and that he could not tolerate the machine well.
Doctor said he was not putting a name/diagnosis on this today.
Doctor advised to go to emergency if he becomes markedly more confused, has a fall, or develops any weakness.
